content: Histopathology, derived from the Greek words histos (tissue) and pathos (suffering), involves the microscopic examination of tissues to study the manifestations of disease. In clinical medicine, histopathology specifically refers to the analysis of biopsy or surgical specimens by a pathologist after the tissue has been processed and histological sections have been mounted onto glass slides. This technique is a cornerstone of anatomical pathology and is essential for the routine clinical diagnosis of cancer and other diseases. Collection of Tissues The histopathological examination begins with the collection of tissue through surgery, biopsy, or autopsy. Once removed, the tissue is placed in a fixative to stabilize it and prevent decay. The most commonly used fixative is formalin, which is a 10% solution of formaldehyde in water. Preparation for Histology The collected tissue undergoes preparation for microscopic examination through histological procedures. Initially, the tissue samples are placed into a cassette, a container designed to allow reagents to act freely on the tissue. The cassette is then immersed in a series of baths containing progressively concentrated ethanol to dehydrate the tissue, followed by toluene or xylene, and finally hot liquid paraffin. This process, known as tissue processing, replaces the water in the tissue with paraffin, a type of wax, turning the soft, moist tissue into a paraffin-compatible sample. This step typically takes 12 to 16 hours. After processing, the tissue is removed from the cassette and embedded in a mold with additional paraffin to create a paraffin block. This embedding process allows the tissue to be sectioned into extremely thin slices, typically 2 to 7 micrometers thick, using a microtome. These thin sections are then placed on glass slides for staining. Staining To visualize the tissue under a microscope, the sections are stained with one or more pigments. Staining highlights cellular components, and counterstains are often used to provide contrast. The most commonly used stain in histopathology is hematoxylin and eosin (H&E). Hematoxylin stains cell nuclei blue, while eosin stains the cytoplasm and extracellular connective tissue matrix pink. In addition to H&E, numerous other staining techniques exist to selectively highlight specific cellular structures. Examples include safranin, Oil Red O, Congo red, silver salts, and artificial dyes. Histochemistry, the science of using chemical reactions to identify tissue components, is also employed. A well-known histochemical technique is the Perls Prussian Blue reaction, which detects iron deposits in conditions such as hemochromatosis. More recently, immunohistochemistry has become a powerful tool in histopathology. This technique uses antibodies to stain specific proteins, lipids, or carbohydrates, significantly enhancing the ability to identify particular cell types under the microscope. Advanced methods like in situ hybridization are also used to detect specific DNA or RNA molecules. Additionally, digital cameras are increasingly utilized to capture histopathological images for analysis and documentation. Interpretation The stained histological slides are examined under a microscope by a pathologist, a medically trained specialist. The pathologist formulates a diagnosis based on the histological findings, which is documented in a pathology report. This report includes a detailed description of the findings and the pathologist's expert opinion. In cases of cancer, the pathology report provides the tissue diagnosis necessary for determining appropriate treatment protocols.
